piece.caption: How to secure WhatsApp Web on shared office computers and prevent data leakage. If your shop staff or billing counter operators leave WhatsApp Web open on shared PCs, anyone can access customer lists, quotations, and pending ledger details. The Ministry of Home Affairs I4C unit warns that closing the tab does not log you out. Always click Log Out manually after your shift, or use private browsing mode for temporary sessions. Have you ever noticed active WhatsApp sessions left open on your office computers? Comment SAFETY for Home Ministry WhatsApp safety guide

claims.claim: I4C under the Ministry of Home Affairs issued an advisory warning that active WhatsApp Web browser sessions on shared computers can be misused to access accounts and contacts.
Closing a browser tab or window does not automatically log out a user from WhatsApp Web.
Active sessions allow attackers to read messages, access contact lists, and impersonate users for fraud or social engineering.
I4C recommends manually logging out after work and using private/incognito browsing mode when temporary access on shared PCs is necessary.
Malicious ZIP files disguised as official communications can install malware on Windows PCs to hijack active WhatsApp Web sessions.

piece.dm_text: Here is the Home Ministry (I4C) WhatsApp Web safety checklist for your office: 1. Always manually log out of WhatsApp Web instead of just closing the browser tab. 2. Avoid exchanging sensitive financial or confidential data on shared PCs via WhatsApp Web. 3. Use Incognito/Private browsing mode when accessing WhatsApp Web on temporary or shared PCs, and log out before closing. 4. Never open unknown ZIP files (disguised as MCA/RBI notices) that install session-hijacking malware. 5. Independently verify urgent payment or fund transfer requests with a direct phone call.

SUMMARY The Home Ministry’s I4C has warned that active WhatsApp Web sessions could be misused to access accounts, read conversations, and impersonate users
Access to a genuine account can help fraudsters exploit the trust of its contacts, exposing personal conversations and business communications to impersonation and financial fraud.
The agency has recommended manually logging out after each session, avoiding public or untrusted computers, and using private browsing on trusted devices when temporary access is unavoidable

The Indian Cyber Crime Coordination Centre (I4C), under the Ministry of Home Affairs, has advised users to avoid exchanging official, financial, confidential, or other sensitive information through WhatsApp Web, warning that active browser sessions could be misused to access their accounts.
In a recent advisory, I4C’s National Cybercrime Threat Analytics Unit (NCTAU) said such access could allow attackers to read messages, impersonate account holders, and access contacts and group conversations. They could then exploit the account holder’s trusted identity for fraud, phishing, and social engineering. The agency urged users to exercise particular caution on office computers, shared systems, public computers, and devices accessible to other people. It also stressed that closing a browser tab or window should not be treated as logging out of WhatsApp Web.
Notably, WhatsApp Web allows users to access the messaging service through a computer browser after linking their account.
I4C has recommended the following measures:
Avoid sensitive work: Government, organisational, financial, confidential, or other sensitive information should preferably not be exchanged through WhatsApp Web on computers.
Limit active sessions: Avoid leaving WhatsApp Web logged in when it is not required, particularly on office or shared computers.
Log out manually: Log out after completing your work rather than simply closing the browser tab or window.
Use private browsing cautiously: If temporary access is unavoidable, use incognito or private browsing mode on a trusted computer and manually log out before closing the browser.
Avoid untrusted computers: Do not access WhatsApp Web from cyber cafes, public kiosks, hotel business centres, borrowed computers, or other untrusted systems.
Watch for unusual activity: Treat unexpected messages sent from your account, unusual replies from contacts, or unexplained activity seriously.
Keep devices secure: Update operating systems, browsers, and security software, and avoid suspicious downloads, unknown files, pirated software, and untrusted applications.
The warning follows an earlier I4C alert about a fraud campaign targeting company directors, finance professionals, and businesspersons through WhatsApp account takeovers.
In August, the agency described how attackers circulated malicious ZIP files disguised as account statements or communications from the RBI and the Ministry of Corporate Affairs. Opening the files on a Windows computer installed malware that could hijack an active WhatsApp Web session.
I4C advised companies to independently verify urgent fund-transfer instructions or requests to change bank account details through a direct voice call or in-person confirmation before acting. Separately, I4C has also flagged the use of AI agents in attacks targeting financial institutions.
The agency recently warned banks, NBFCs, and fintech startups about attackers exploiting unpatched software and misconfigured internet-facing servers to access financial infrastructure. The warnings also come amid efforts to strengthen safeguards on messaging platforms. It was reported last month that platforms including WhatsApp and Telegram were preparing to implement the Department of Telecommunications’ SIM-binding mandate .
